name: Learn: AppArmor Confinement
description: Confine containers with AppArmor step by step — write and load a profile on a node with apparmor_parser, reference it from a pod via securityContext.appArmorProfile, verify a denied action is blocked, and contrast confined vs unconfined pods. Exam-focused runtime-security practice.
objective: CKS › System Hardening (15%). Goal: write and load an AppArmor profile on a node, reference it from a pod (localhost/<name>), prove a denied operation is blocked, and contrast confined vs unconfined workloads — the mandatory-access-control hardening the exam expects.

questions.title: Load an AppArmor profile on a node
questions.teach:
**AppArmor** is a Linux Security Module (LSM) providing **Mandatory Access Control (MAC)** — it confines a program to a set of allowed operations by *path* (contrast SELinux, which is label-based). A **profile** names the program and lists rules such as `deny /etc/secret-data/** w,` (deny writes under that path).

**Profile modes** — know all three:
- **enforce**: violations are *blocked* and logged (what this lab uses).
- **complain**: violations are *allowed* but logged — use it to learn what a profile needs, then promote to enforce.
- **unconfined**: no restrictions at all.

**Loading / managing profiles** (all on the node):
- `apparmor_parser -r /etc/apparmor.d/<file>` — (re)load a profile into the kernel. `-W` waits for completion; `-R` removes one.
- `aa-status` (a.k.a. `apparmor_status`) — list loaded profiles and their modes.
- `aa-complain <profile>` / `aa-enforce <profile>` — flip a profile's mode (from the `apparmor-utils` package).

**GOTCHAS**
- The kernel tracks a profile by its **profile name** (the string after the `profile` keyword), *not* the filename — by convention they match, but a pod references the **name**.
- A profile must be loaded on **every node** the pod might land on (profiles are node-local, not in the API server). If the profile is missing, the kubelet refuses to start the pod.
- AppArmor must be enabled in the kernel: check `cat /sys/module/apparmor/parameters/enabled` returns `Y` (or `aa-enabled`).
- Profile rule syntax is strict: every rule ends with a comma; `deny` lines, globs (`**` recursive, `*` single level), and permission flags (`r w a x m l k`) all matter.

This step is **RUNTIME**: `apparmor_parser` and the kernel LSM must exist on the host. We validate that the profile file is present on the node with the correct `deny ... w,` rule.
questions.prompt:
On worker node `$W1`, create an AppArmor profile file at `/etc/apparmor.d/k8s-deny-write` with profile name `k8s-deny-write` that **denies all writes** to files under `/etc/secret-data/`, then load it with `apparmor_parser`.

Target: the file `/etc/apparmor.d/k8s-deny-write` exists on `$W1` and contains a `deny` write rule for `/etc/secret-data/`.
questions.hint:
Use a heredoc through `docker exec -i "$W1" tee /etc/apparmor.d/k8s-deny-write`. The profile body: `#include <tunables/global>` then `profile k8s-deny-write flags=(attach_disconnected) { #include <abstractions/base>
  file,
  deny /etc/secret-data/** w,
}`. Load with `docker exec "$W1" apparmor_parser -r -W /etc/apparmor.d/k8s-deny-write`.

verification.description: profile /etc/apparmor.d/k8s-deny-write with a deny-write rule exists on $W1

questions.title: Reference the profile from a pod
questions.teach:
A pod tells the kubelet which AppArmor profile to apply **per-container**. On modern Kubernetes (1.30+, GA) use the typed field `securityContext.appArmorProfile`; the pre-1.30 way was an **annotation** — recognise both because old exam docs/manifests still use annotations.

**appArmorProfile `type` values** — the three you must know:
- `Localhost` — use a profile already loaded on the node; requires `localhostProfile: <profile-name>` (here `k8s-deny-write`). The value is the **profile name**, *not* a file path.
- `RuntimeDefault` — apply the container runtime's default AppArmor profile; no name needed.
- `Unconfined` — disable AppArmor for the container (no confinement).

**Pod-level vs container-level** — `appArmorProfile` can be set under `spec.securityContext` (pod-level default for all containers) **or** `spec.containers[].securityContext` (container-level, which overrides the pod-level value). The beta annotation was container-only.

**Equivalent annotation** (deprecated since 1.30; still read for backward compatibility, but the typed `appArmorProfile` field takes precedence): `container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/<container-name>: localhost/<profile-name>` — note the `localhost/` prefix and that it's keyed by **container name**.

**GOTCHAS**
- `localhost` means “a profile already present on this node” — which is why Step 1 had to load it. If the profile isn't loaded, the pod stays **Blocked/won't start** (describe shows the reason).
- The pod must be **scheduled onto the node that has the profile** — here we pin it with `nodeName: $W1` (bypasses the scheduler). In the real world you'd load the profile on all candidate nodes instead.
- Don't mix the typed field and the annotation on the same container with conflicting values.
- The annotation's `<container-name>` suffix and the `localhost/` prefix are easy to typo — a mistake silently leaves the container unconfined (annotation) or blocks the pod.
questions.prompt:
In namespace `cks-apparmor`, create a pod `confined` pinned to node `$W1`, image `busybox:1.36`, command `sleep 3600`, whose container `hello` references the **localhost** AppArmor profile `k8s-deny-write`.

Target: pod `confined` is on `$W1` and its container requests the localhost profile `k8s-deny-write` (via `appArmorProfile` or the beta annotation).
questions.hint: Set `spec.containers[0].securityContext.appArmorProfile: { type: Localhost, localhostProfile: k8s-deny-write }` and `spec.nodeName: $W1`. (Equivalent annotation: `container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/hello: localhost/k8s-deny-write`.)
questions.solution:
cat <<YAML | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: confined
  namespace: cks-apparmor
spec:
  nodeName: $W1
  containers:
  - name: hello
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep","3600"]
    securityContext:
      appArmorProfile:
        type: Localhost
        localhostProfile: k8s-deny-write
YAML

verification.description: pod 'confined' on $W1 references localhost profile k8s-deny-write

questions.title: Verify the confinement blocks a write
questions.teach:
On an AppArmor-capable node the loaded profile actually **blocks** the denied action. Prove it: run a write inside the confined pod and record the result — a real host returns `Permission denied`. (On this Mac there's no AppArmor, so the write would succeed — that's why this is a requires-host step.)

**Ways to verify confinement is active:**
- Trigger the denied operation from inside the pod: `kubectl exec <pod> -- sh -c 'touch /etc/secret-data/x'` → expect `Permission denied` (exit non-zero).
- `kubectl get pod <pod> -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[0].securityContext.appArmorProfile}'` — confirm the spec still requests the profile.
- On the node: `aa-status` lists the profile in **enforce** mode; denials are logged to the kernel audit log — `dmesg | grep -i apparmor` or `/var/log/audit/audit.log` shows `apparmor="DENIED"` entries with `operation=`, `profile=`, `name=`.

**GOTCHAS**
- A profile in **complain** mode logs the violation but does **not** block it — the write succeeds. Check the mode with `aa-status` if an expected denial doesn't happen.
- The deny rule is **path-based**: `deny /etc/secret-data/** w,` blocks writes under that exact path only. A write to `/tmp` is *not* covered by that rule and may succeed (depending on the base profile). Match the test path to the rule you wrote.
- If the profile isn't loaded on the node, the pod never starts — you'd see a kubelet error, not a `Permission denied` from inside a running container.
- `type: RuntimeDefault` or `Unconfined` would not enforce your custom rule — only `Localhost` with the right profile name does.
questions.prompt:
Run a write to the **protected** path inside the `confined` pod (`touch /etc/secret-data/x`) and capture its output into a ConfigMap `apparmor-proof` (key `result`) in `cks-apparmor`.

Target: ConfigMap `apparmor-proof` exists and its `result` shows the write was denied (contains `Permission denied`).
questions.hint: `kubectl -n cks-apparmor create configmap apparmor-proof --from-literal=result="$(kubectl -n cks-apparmor exec confined -- sh -c 'touch /etc/secret-data/x' 2>&1)"` — write to a path the profile denies (`/etc/secret-data/`), not `/tmp` (which the profile allows).
questions.solution:
kubectl -n cks-apparmor create configmap apparmor-proof \
  --from-literal=result="$(kubectl -n cks-apparmor exec confined -- sh -c 'touch /etc/secret-data/x' 2>&1)"
# on an AppArmor host the result is: touch: /etc/secret-data/x: Permission denied

verification.description: confined container still bound to profile k8s-deny-write (enforcement needs host)

questions.title: Contrast: unconfined vs confined
questions.teach:
To appreciate what AppArmor buys you, compare two pods. A container with **no** AppArmor setting (or `type: Unconfined`) runs under the host's default/unconfined policy — the write to `/etc/secret-data/` would **succeed**. The confined pod from Step 2 blocks it. **Three ways a container ends up unconfined** (recognise each): - No `appArmorProfile` and no annotation at all → whatever the runtime defaults to (often `RuntimeDefault` or unconfined depending on config). - `appArmorProfile.type: Unconfined` → explicitly disabled. - Annotation `container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/: unconfined`. **Inspecting pods quickly** (exam reflexes): - `kubectl get pod

-o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[0].securityContext.appArmorProfile}'` — prints the typed field (empty for unconfined). - `kubectl get pod

-o yaml | grep -i apparmor` — catches *both* the typed field and the beta annotation. - Across a namespace: `kubectl get pods -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,APP:'.spec.containers[*].securityContext.appArmorProfile.localhostProfile'`. **GOTCHAS** - An empty jsonpath result is ambiguous — it could mean unconfined *or* that the setting lives in the beta annotation instead of the typed field. Always check both. - `Unconfined` on one container does **not** affect sibling containers — AppArmor is per-container. - A pod-level `appArmorProfile` applies to every container *unless* a container overrides it; so “unconfined” at container level can still override a confining pod-level default. - Least privilege means the profile is applied **deliberately**, not everywhere by accident — the exam tests that you can confirm exactly which workloads carry a restrictive profile.
questions.prompt:
In namespace `cks-apparmor`, create a second pod `unconfined` on node `$W1`, image `busybox:1.36`, command `sleep 3600`, with **no** AppArmor localhost profile (leave it unset, or set `type: Unconfined`).

Target: `unconfined` does NOT reference `k8s-deny-write`, while `confined` (Step 2) still does — the two pods differ in their AppArmor setting.
questions.hint: Just omit the `appArmorProfile`/annotation on `unconfined` (or set `appArmorProfile.type: Unconfined`). The validator confirms `confined` has the localhost profile and `unconfined` does not.
questions.solution:
cat <<YAML | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: unconfined
  namespace: cks-apparmor
spec:
  nodeName: $W1
  containers:
  - name: hello
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep","3600"]
YAML
# Compare:
kubectl -n cks-apparmor get pod confined   -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[0].securityContext.appArmorProfile}{"\n"}'
kubectl -n cks-apparmor get pod unconfined -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[0].securityContext.appArmorProfile}{"\n"}'

verification.description: confined uses k8s-deny-write; unconfined does not (the two differ)
